# Working with Spatial Data in R - Vector Data

## Highlights

- Vector data represent spatial features as **geometries**: points, lines, and polygons.
  - *Point* = single coordinate pair
  - *Line* = sequence of coordinate pairs
  - *Polygon* = sequence of coordinate pairs, with the last overlapping the first.
- Geometries are stored as coordinate pairs in their own column in a **spatial dataframe**.
- Geometries and spatial dataframes are also associated with a **coordinate reference system** (crs)
  - The crs defines origin and axes to which the coordinate pairs are referenced.
  - A crs can be geographic and use angular units (e.g. latitude/longitude) ;\
    Or it can be projected and use linear units (e.g. UTM, State Plane)

By the end, you should be able to create points from a table, inspect their CRS, display an interactive map, and attach county attributes using a spatial join.

```{r setup}
#Import packages
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(fs)
library(sf)

#Disable geodesic/force planar calculations
#sf_use_s2(FALSE)

## Mapview is a simple package for making interactive maps ##
#install.packages(mapview)
library(mapview)
mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap","Esri.WorldImagery"))

#Local Paths
raw_folder = here('Data/raw')
processed_folder = here('Data/processed')
```

## Reading in spatial data

### Converting a dataframe with coordinate data to a spatial dataframe

If your dataframe has coordinate data, i.e., columns for X and Y coordinates, you can convert the dataframe to a spatial dataframe by building point geometries from those coordinate data. Here we read in the `NWIS_SiteInfo_NE_RAW.csv` file, which has an "x" (`dec_long_va`) and a "y" (`dec_lat_va`) column, and convert it to a spatial dataframe via the `st_as_sf()` function.

Note we have to also provide the coordinate reference system (crs). We do so by providing its EPSG code; our data has coordinates that are latitude/longitude, so we use the EPSG code of 4326 which represents the World Geodetic Survey of 1984. (See <https://epsg.io/>).

Note also, we run `st_make_valid()` on the spatial dataframe to ensure its geometry is valid.

```{r table to spatial df}
#First read in the file as a dataframe
NWIS_filename <- here(raw_folder,'NWIS_SiteInfo_NE_RAW.csv')
NWIS_df <- read.csv(NWIS_filename)

#Then convert to a spatial dataframe using `st_as_sf`, 
# specifying the coordinate fields and the crs
NWIS_sdf <- st_as_sf(
  x = NWIS_df, 
  coords = c('dec_long_va','dec_lat_va'),
  crs = 4326
) |> st_make_valid()

#View the dataframe with MapView
mapview(NWIS_sdf)

```

### Reading GeoJSON files directly from the internet

GeoJSON is a text file format that stores all the information of a geospatial feature class: geometries, attributes, and coordinate reference system information. The are text based equivalents of Shapefiles, but since they have all the data in a single file, they are a bit easier to work with. In fact, a web site can host these data on-line and we can read them directly into a spatial dataframe using `st_read()`.

A quick web search for "US Counties GeoJSON" reveals many sources of that dataset. The one that pop up in the result for me is: <https://eric.clst.org/tech/usgeojson/> - an individual who has decided to host many datasets on his personal web site.

The link for US Counties at a 1:5m scale is: [`https://eric.clst.org/assets/wiki/uploads/Stuff/gz_2010_us_050_00_5m.json`](https://eric.clst.org/assets/wiki/uploads/Stuff/gz_2010_us_050_00_5m.json).

We'll fetch that, reading its contents into a spatial dataframe, filtering for just counties in Nebraska, whose state FIPS code is "31". Again, we pass the result to the `st_make_valid()` function to ensure its geometry is valid.

```{r reading GeoJSON files}
counties_sdf <- st_read(
  dsn='https://eric.clst.org/assets/wiki/uploads/Stuff/gz_2010_us_050_00_5m.json',
) |> 
  #Filter for Nebraska
  filter(STATE == '31')|> st_make_valid()

#Reveal the crs the datasets uses
st_crs(counties_sdf)

#Display the results
mapview(counties_sdf) + 
  mapview(NWIS_sdf,col.regions='red')
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Spatial Operations

### Spatial Join

A spatial join assigns values in one dataset based on its overlap with a second spatial dataset. For example, if we wanted to tag each of our NWIS points with the county in which it falls, we would *spatially join* the county data to the points. This is done via the `st_join()` function.

```{r spatial join}
#Spatially join 
NWIS_joined <- st_join(
  x = NWIS_sdf,        #The target sdf to receive the attributes
  y = counties_sdf,    #The join sdf to supply the attributes
  join = st_intersects #The predicate: how the data should be related
)

#See that the fields have been joined
str(NWIS_joined)

#View the points, now sized by CENSUSAREA and colored by COUNTY
ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = counties_sdf,color='grey') +
  geom_sf(data = NWIS_joined,aes(size=CENSUSAREA,color=COUNTY)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
  
```

### Spatial Filtering

We can also select features in one spatial dataframe based on its relationship to features in another dataframe. This is a straightforward operation using the `st_filter()` function.

First, we'll fetch some HUC (drainage area) data from <https://data.openwaterfoundation.org/country/us/usgs/huc-basins/>. Specifically, we'll get the Platte River HUC4 (1020): [`https://data.openwaterfoundation.org/country/us/usgs/huc-basins/huc4-basin-1020-platte.geojson`](https://data.openwaterfoundation.org/country/us/usgs/huc-basins/huc4-basin-1020-platte.geojson){.uri}

```{r Fetch HUC 4}
#Fetch the North Platte HUC4 
huc4_url = 'https://data.openwaterfoundation.org/country/us/usgs/huc-basins/huc4-basin-1020-platte.geojson'
huc4_sdf = st_read(huc4_url) |> st_make_valid()

#Display the HUC4 with the NWIS points
mapview(huc4_sdf) + 
  mapview(NWIS_joined,
          col.regions='red', #Color the points red
          cex=2)             #Set size of the points to 2
```

Now, we'll filter the NWIS sites, selecting only those that intersect the features in the Platte River HUC4.

```{r}
#Filter the NWIS sites that intersect the Platte River HUC4
NWIS_selected <- st_filter(
    x = NWIS_joined, 
    y = huc4_sdf,
    .predicate = st_intersects
    )

#Display
#Display the HUC4 with the NWIS points
mapview(huc4_sdf) + 
  mapview(NWIS_joined,col.regions='gray', cex=2) +
  mapview(NWIS_selected,col.regions='red', cex=3) 
```

Note the last argument - `.predicate = st_intersects`. This defines how the features are selected, i.e. NWIS points that spatially *intersect* the HUC4. There are other predicates listed on the [sf cheat sheet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/sf.pdf).

### Clipping Features

In addition to spatially selecting features, we can clip features in one spatial dataframe using features in another. Here we'll clip the counties to areas that intersect the Platte River HUC4.

```{r Clip Features}
counties_clip <- st_intersection(
  x = counties_sdf, 
  y = huc4_sdf
)

#Plot (mapview won't work b/c of duplicate field names)
ggplot() + geom_sf(data=counties_clip)

```

### Spatial Selection & Aggregation

We use `st_filter` to subset features spatially and write output to a new file. However, if we just want to spatially select a subset of features in an existing spatial dataframe, we use a different approach.

In this example, we'll assign a value to each county indicating if it touches the HUC4.

```{r}
#Initialize the column values "OUT:
counties_HUC <- counties_sdf |> mutate(InHUC = "OUT")
#Next we create a Boolean mask of counties that intersect the HUC4
counties_intersect_mask <- st_intersects(
  x = counties_HUC, 
  y = huc4_sdf, 
  sparse = FALSE
)
#We update records where the mask is true
counties_HUC[counties_intersect_mask,'InHUC'] = "IN"

#Show results
mapview(counties_HUC,zcol='InHUC')
```

You can group spatial dataframes just as you would a tabular one, just that when you do, all geometries with a common grouped value will merge into a single spatial feature. If two spatial features share a boundary, that boundary will be *dissolved*, i.e., it will disappear.

```{r}
#Select NE Counties that intersect the Platte R. HUC4
counties_HUC_dissolved <- counties_HUC |> 
  group_by(InHUC) |> 
  summarize(
    #Update the area
    CENSUSAREA=sum(CENSUSAREA)
  )

mapview(counties_HUC_dissolved,zcol='InHUC')
```

### Geometry manipulations

We can alter the geometries in a spatial dataframe. For example, we can buffer features or reduce polygons to their centroids. In doing these calculations, however, we want to ensure our data use a ***projected coordinate reference system***, i.e., one where the x's and y's are in **linear units** (meters or feet) and not **angular units** (latitude/longitude).

Without going into gory detail, you'll want to **transform** your data to a **UTM coordinate system**. Because we are in Nebraska, we'll use UTM Zone 14N, whose EPSG code is [32614](https://epsg.io/32614).

```{r Transform datasets}
#Transform our datasets to use UTM Zone 14N coordinates
NWIS_utm <- st_transform(NWIS_joined, crs = 32614)
counties_utm <- st_transform(counties_sdf, crs = 32614)
hucs_utm <- st_transform(huc4_sdf, crs=32614)

#Check
st_crs(NWIS_utm) == st_crs(counties_utm)
```

Now that the geometry are in meters, we sensibly measure distances between objects and buffer.

Here are some examples:

```{r Geometry manipulations}
#Plot
myMap = ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = counties_utm)
myMap

#Extract the centroids of the selected features and show them
county_centroids <-  st_centroid(counties_utm)
myMap <- myMap + geom_sf(data = county_centroids, color = 'blue')
myMap

#Buffer the centroids outward 5km and add them to our
county_centroids_8km <- st_buffer(county_centroids, 8000)
myMap <- myMap + geom_sf(data = county_centroids_8km, color = 'orange', fill=NA)
myMap

#Buffer the counties inward 5km
county_in5km <- st_buffer(counties_utm, -5000)
myMap <- myMap + geom_sf(data = county_in5km, color = 'green', fill=NA)
myMap

#Combine the centroids into one feature and construct a convex hull around them
county_centroids_chull <- county_centroids %>% 
  st_union() %>% 
  st_convex_hull()
myMap <- myMap + geom_sf(data = county_centroids_chull, color = 'red', fill=NA)
myMap

#Combine the centroids into one feature and draw voronoi polygons
county_centroids_voronoi <- county_centroids %>% 
  st_union() %>% 
  st_voronoi()
myMap <- myMap + geom_sf(data = county_centroids_voronoi, color = 'purple', fill=NA)
myMap
```

### Distance calculations

If we want to identify the nearest feature in one dataframe to features in another, we and use `st_join()`, specifying the join to be the nearest features.

```{r Nearest feature}
NWIS_nearest_county <- st_join(
  x = NWIS_utm, 
  y = county_centroids, 
  join = st_nearest_feature)
```

If we want to calculate the distance to the nearest feature as well as assign the name, it's a bit more involved.

```{r}
#Get the index of the closest county centroid to each NWIS point
nearest_county_idx <- st_nearest_feature(
  x = NWIS_utm,
  y = county_centroids,
)

#Assign the name of the county to the NWIS dataframe 
NWIS_utm$closest_county <- county_centroids$NAME[nearest_county_idx]

#Compute distance values
NWIS_utm$distance_to_nearest_co <- st_distance(
  NWIS_utm, 
  county_centroids[nearest_county_idx, ], 
  by_element = TRUE) |> as.numeric()

ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(
    data = counties_utm
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data=county_centroids,color='black',shape='x'
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = NWIS_utm,
    aes(size = distance_to_nearest_co)
  ) 

```
